intro: A civil marriage law open to any two people regardless of religion — commonly used for inter-faith marriages, or by anyone who wants a non-religious registered marriage.

sections.p: Neither party has a living spouse; both can give valid consent; the man is at least 21 and the woman at least 18; and they're not within prohibited degrees of relationship (unless custom permits).
The couple gives written notice to the Marriage Officer of the district where at least one of them has lived for the last 30 days.

The notice is displayed in the Marriage Officer's office. Anyone can object within 30 days, but only on the ground that a legal condition (S 4) isn't met. The officer must inquire and decide within 30 days.

After 30 days without valid objection, the marriage is solemnised before the Marriage Officer and three witnesses, and a marriage certificate is entered in the register — conclusive proof of marriage.
Couples already married under other rites can register their marriage under this Act if the conditions are met.

Marriage under this Act severs a Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh or Jain party from their joint family. Succession to the couple's property is governed by the Indian Succession Act — except where both parties are Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh or Jain, in which case Hindu succession law applies (S 21A).

Similar to the Hindu Marriage Act: adultery, desertion for 2 years, cruelty, imprisonment for 7 years or more, incurable unsound mind, communicable venereal disease, not heard of for 7 years, and non-resumption of cohabitation after a separation or restitution decree.
If the couple has lived separately for a year and agrees the marriage should end, they can file jointly; the decree is passed after a 6-month waiting period (which courts can waive).
